claude.sample_unit: community health worker questions with responses rated

links.outcome: Consistency and agreement of expert clinician raters used as reference standard
links.effect: Expert clinician ratings described as highly inconsistent; best LLM-judge matched human-equivalent evaluation on only four of eleven criteria.
links.quote: These findings underscore the need for further investment in scalable evaluation solutions, as well as potentially a fundamental rethink of how we approach the concept of “correctness” in clinical AI assessment (which is currently based on highly inconsistent expert clinician raters).

unlisted_practices: Using LLM-as-a-judge and LLM juries to scale evaluation of generative AI outputs

links.effect: Claude-4.1-Opus achieved human-equivalent evaluations on only four of eleven criteria.
links.quote: Our results show that even the highest-performing LLM-judge (Claude-4.1-Opus) achieved human-equivalent evaluations on only four of eleven criteria.

links.effect: Performance and cost-effectiveness deteriorated substantially moving from English to Kinyarwanda inputs.
links.quote: Moreover, performance and cost-effectiveness deteriorated substantially when moving from English to Kinyarwanda inputs.

links.effect: LLM juries improved agreement on only one additional criterion; GPT-5 was overcritical and Gemini-2.5-Pro overly lenient.
links.quote: Constructing “LLM juries” to balance model-specific biases improved agreement on only one additional criterion.
